title: Why A Letter Home Is An Effective Consequence https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/07/03/why-a-letter-home-is-an-effective-consequence/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin recommends a letter home as the third consequence in a classroom management plan, but stresses its value lies less in the punishment itself than in the accountability it creates. He details the mechanics: use an impersonal form letter, hand it to the student immediately upon the third rule violation of the day, and follow up with a phone call if it isn't returned signed the next day. Because the plan and a sample letter are included in the first-week parent packet, neither students nor parents should be caught off guard when a letter arrives. Linsin lists three reasons the letter works: it satisfies parents' right to be informed of problems, it hands the student a genuine act of responsibility in delivering it, and it forces full accountability to the teacher, the parents, and the student themselves.
points: A letter home works best as the third consequence in a classroom management plan, following a warning and time-out.
Use an impersonal, official-looking form letter and hand it to the student immediately after the third rule violation of the day.
If the signed letter isn't returned the next day, follow up with a phone call; consistent follow-through usually prevents repeat testing.
Include the classroom management plan and a sample letter in the first-week parent packet so neither students nor parents are surprised.
The letter works because it satisfies parents' right to know, gives students a genuine act of responsibility, and forces accountability to teacher, parents, and self.
quotes: I can’t emphasize enough that consequences for misbehavior are only a small part of classroom management. By themselves, they cannot deter students from misbehaving.
A form letter—official looking and impersonal—strikes the right tone in communicating the seriousness of breaking rules and interrupting learning.
If you don’t get the letter back the next day, simply follow up with a phone call. Chances are you’re being tested.
If a child breaks your classroom rules three times in one day, his or her parents have a right to know.
They’re accountable to you because they must get the letter signed and returned—honoring and respecting your authority.
And they’re accountable to themselves—understanding that there are consequences for the choices they make.
